text:
I've been slowly adding to $ONDS again because after  years of acquisitions across autonomous defense I think we're finally reaching the point where we get to see whether all those pieces can form a real platform.

The company now has counter-drone systems, long-endurance surveillance through ULTRA and World View, Mistral's defense relationships, ground robotics and a growing software layer through $PLTR, Omnisys, DefenseOS and Regna that could connect everything together.

The upside could be massive as modern warfare shifts toward coordinated autonomous systems across air and ground so Ondas has essentially bought all the pieces it needed to become a serious player but now they have to prove they built a company.

text:

Only fair for me to highlight both the successes AND the struggles of the traders I work with as I try to convey the authentic truth of being a trader.

On the SMB call we will discuss what has been working well, what hasn’t been, and how best to adapt. Soliciting feedback across teams and individuals.

Here is the main message I will be conveying to their traders which I think is useful for all to hear:

IMO, the most common issues I’m seeing is that traders are getting overly involved and over-allocating risk to situations that had potential but never unfolded optimally.

$BWET is a name that got extended, but never enough to take a real stand.

The breakouts in $QQQ or certain single-stock names had solid charts but the breadth beneath the market was awful. We still had yellow lights flashing in certain areas.

The recent AI sell-off was extended and had its moments, but it lacked the intraday flush or intraday setups to size into anything.

When these setups have unfolded suboptimally, traders have continued to stay involved and allocate risk in a refusal to acknowledge that the setup is not as good as it had the potential to be.

I’d argue this comes down to maintaining an objectively high level of subjectivity. Selectivity is staying in your lane and

name: Business Breakdowns
zh_summary: (Reposted by @patrick_oshag) @bizbreakdowns breaks down $AFRM with Fraser Christie of Sandstone Global Investment, who believes Affirm can become the payment network of the internet. Points include: the stock fell more than 95% after its 2021 IPO, it now processes over $50B in GMV growing more than 30%, holds about 50% of US buy now pay later, earns about 4% gross profit on volume, and Affirm Card is about 20% of volume growing over 100% a year.
en_summary: (Reposted by @patrick_oshag) @bizbreakdowns breaks down $AFRM with Fraser Christie of Sandstone Global Investment, who believes Affirm can become the payment network of the internet. Points include: the stock fell more than 95% after its 2021 IPO, it now processes over $50B in GMV growing more than 30%, holds about 50% of US buy now pay later, earns about 4% gross profit on volume, and Affirm Card is about 20% of volume growing over 100% a year.
text:
Today, we are breaking down @Affirm.
 
Affirm's stock fell more than 95% after its IPO in 2021. Today, it processes over $50 billion in GMV and is growing more than 30%, faster than when it was a fraction of its current size.

Its founder, Max Levchin (@mlevchin), grew up in Ukraine, moved to the US as a teenager, and co-founded PayPal in his early 20s. 

While in college, he funded his first startups with credit cards and unknowingly destroyed his credit score. Years later, even after PayPal's IPO, he was denied a car loan because of his credit history. 

That experience helped inspire Affirm's founding mission of building more honest financial products.

Fraser Christie, founder and CIO of Sandstone Global Investment, joined us to break down the business, its remarkable recovery, and why he believes Affirm can become the payment network of the internet.

Some interesting facts from our conversation:

1/ Affirm has roughly 50% market share in US buy now, pay later

2/ Max Levchin earns less than $40,000 in annual salary and owns billions in Affirm stock. He now spends much of his time working with a small engineering team on new products.

3/ Affirm can have negative customer acquisition costs. 

4/ 70% of purchase volume comes from interest-bearing loans

5/ Affirm earns roughly 4% gross profit on purchase volume after funding costs and credit losses.

6/ Affirm underwrites every transaction individually

7/ Affirm Card already accounts for roughly 20% of purchase volume an
